paragraphs: Paul looked straight at the council members and said his piece: "Friends, I've lived with a clear conscience before God my whole life, right up to this very moment." That set off the high priest Ananias. He ordered his aides to slap Paul across the face. Paul fired back, "God is going to strike you down! What a hypocrite you are! You sit there judging me by the Law, then break the Law by ordering me slapped!"
The aides were shocked: "How dare you talk to God's high priest like that!"

Paul acted surprised. "How was I supposed to know he was the high priest? He sure doesn't act like one. You're right — Scripture does say, 'Don't speak evil of a ruler of your people.' Sorry about that."

Paul knew the council was split between Sadducees and Pharisees — and how much they despised each other — so he decided to use their rivalry: "Friends, I'm a die-hard Pharisee from a long line of Pharisees. I'm on trial here because of my Pharisee beliefs — the hope of the resurrection of the dead."

The second he said that, the council split down the middle, Pharisees and Sadducees going at each other in a heated shouting match. The Sadducees don't believe in resurrection, angels, or spirits — if they can't see it, they don't buy it. The Pharisees believe in all of it. So a massive, noisy brawl broke out. Then some of the Pharisee legal experts shouted the others down: "We don't find anything wrong with this man! What if a spirit spoke to him? Or an angel? What if we end up fighting against God?"

That threw gasoline on the fire. The fight flared up so violently the commander was afraid they'd tear Paul limb from limb. He ordered the soldiers to pull him out of there and escort him back to the safety of the barracks.

That night the Master came to Paul in a vision: "Don't be afraid. It's all going to work out. You've been a faithful witness for me here in Jerusalem — and now you're going to witness for me in Rome!"

The next day, the Jews hatched a plot against Paul. They took a solemn oath not to eat or drink until they'd killed him. More than forty of them bound themselves to this murder pact and went to the chief priests and elders. "We've sworn a solemn oath to eat nothing until we've killed Paul. But we need your help. Have the council ask the commander to bring Paul down tomorrow, as if you want to investigate the charges more carefully. We'll handle the rest. Before he gets anywhere near you, we'll kill him. Your hands stay clean."

But Paul's nephew — his sister's son — overheard them planning the ambush. He went straight to the barracks and told Paul. Paul called over one of the centurions and said, "Take this young man to the commander. He's got something important to tell him."
The centurion took him to the commander and said, "The prisoner Paul asked me to bring this young man to you — he has something urgent to report."
The commander took the young man by the arm and led him aside privately. "What is it? What do you need to tell me?"

Paul's nephew said, "The Jews have cooked up a plot against Paul. Tomorrow morning they're going to ask you to bring Paul to the council, claiming they want to investigate the charges against him more thoroughly. But it's a trap to get him out of your custody so they can kill him. Right now more than forty men are lying in ambush for him. They've all vowed not to eat or drink until they've killed him. Everything's set — they're just waiting for you to send him over."
The commander sent the nephew off with a warning: "Don't breathe a word of this to anyone."

The commander called two centurions. "Get two hundred soldiers ready to leave for Caesarea immediately. Add seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. I want them ready to march by nine o'clock tonight. And get a couple of horses for Paul and his gear. We're delivering this man safe and sound to Governor Felix."

Then he wrote this letter: From Claudius Lysias, to His Excellency Governor Felix: Greetings! I rescued this man from a Jewish mob. They'd grabbed him and were about to kill him when I found out he was a Roman citizen — so I sent in my soldiers. I wanted to know what he'd done wrong, so I brought him before their council. It turned out to be a vicious squabble over their religious differences — nothing even close to a crime. Then I learned they'd cooked up a plot to murder him. I decided the safest move was to get him out of here fast. So I'm sending him to you, and I've told his accusers to present their case before you.

The soldiers followed orders and took Paul that same night to safety in Antipatris. In the morning the foot soldiers returned to their barracks in Jerusalem, while the cavalry escorted Paul on to Caesarea. The horsemen rode into Caesarea and handed Paul and the letter over to the governor.

After reading the letter, the governor asked Paul which province he was from and was told "Cilicia." Then he said, "I'll hear your case when your accusers arrive." He ordered Paul locked up for now in Herod's palace.
title: A Nephew's Tip-Off and a Midnight Rescue
